Lawful Oaths
LAW-ful OHTHS
noun phrase (Christian ethics)
The biblical doctrine that solemn oaths and vows, lawfully taken, are a legitimate and sometimes-required part of Christian life, distinguished from the common profane swearing and the casual oath-taking that Christ forbids (Matthew 5:34-37). The Reformed-confessional position (Westminster Confession XXII) affirms lawful oaths and vows.

Biblical Definition

The biblical doctrine that solemn oaths and vows, lawfully taken, are a legitimate and sometimes-required part of Christian life. The Reformed-confessional position (Westminster Confession XXII, Of Lawful Oaths and Vows) affirms that a lawful oath is a part of religious worship, wherein the person swearing in truth, righteousness, and judgment solemnly calls God to witness what he asserts or promises (XXII.1). The biblical foundation: (1) God Himself swears by His own name (Genesis 22:16; Hebrews 6:13-17, because he could swear by no greater, he sware by himself); (2) the patriarchs, prophets, and apostles took lawful oaths (Abraham, Genesis 21:23-24; the LORD's command to swear by His name, Deuteronomy 6:13; 10:20; Paul's oaths, Romans 1:9; 2 Corinthians 1:23; Galatians 1:20); (3) the third commandment regulates rather than prohibits oath-taking (Exodus 20:7, forbidding the taking of the LORD's name in vain, which presupposes the lawful taking of His name in truth). The Lord Jesus's prohibition in the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5:34-37, swear not at all) is understood by the Reformed-confessional tradition to forbid the casual, profane, evasive, and false oath-taking of the Pharisaic practice (swearing by heaven, earth, Jerusalem, one's head to create gradations of binding-ness and evasion), not to forbid the solemn lawful oath taken in truth before God in appropriate settings (courts of law, ordination, marriage, covenant-membership, etc.). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive Reformed-confessional doctrine: lawful oaths and vows are legitimate and sometimes required; the Christian's ordinary speech should be plain truth requiring no oath (Matthew 5:37, let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay); but the solemn lawful oath in appropriate settings is affirmed against the Anabaptist-Quaker prohibition of all oath-taking.

Webster 1828 Definition

Biblical doctrine that solemn oaths and vows, lawfully taken, are legitimate and sometimes required; Reformed-confessional position (Westminster XXII); God Himself swears (Hebrews 6:13-17); Christ's prohibition (Matthew 5:34-37) forbids casual/profane/evasive oaths, not the solemn lawful oath.

LAWFUL OATHS, n. phr. (Christian ethics) Solemn oaths and vows, lawfully taken, are legitimate and sometimes required. Reformed-confessional position (Westminster XXII): a lawful oath is part of religious worship wherein the swearer solemnly calls God to witness. Foundation: (1) God Himself swears by His own name (Genesis 22:16; Hebrews 6:13-17); (2) patriarchs, prophets, apostles took lawful oaths (Abraham; Deuteronomy 6:13; Paul, Romans 1:9; 2 Corinthians 1:23); (3) the third commandment regulates rather than prohibits oath-taking. Christ's prohibition (Matthew 5:34-37) forbids casual, profane, evasive Pharisaic oath-taking, not the solemn lawful oath in appropriate settings (courts, ordination, marriage, covenant-membership). Affirmed against the Anabaptist-Quaker prohibition of all oaths.

Key Scripture

Hebrews 6:13-17 — "For when God made promise to Abraham, because he could swear by no greater, he sware by himself... Wherein God, willing more abundantly to shew unto the heirs of promise the immutability of his counsel, confirmed it by an oath."

Deuteronomy 6:13 — "Thou shalt fear the LORD thy God, and serve him, and shalt swear by his name."

Matthew 5:34-37 — "But I say unto you, Swear not at all; neither by heaven; for it is God's throne... But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil."

2 Corinthians 1:23 — "Moreover I call God for a record upon my soul, that to spare you I came not as yet unto Corinth."

Modern Corruption

The Anabaptist-Quaker prohibition of all oath-taking misreads Matthew 5:34-37; Christ forbids casual, profane, and evasive oaths, not the solemn lawful oath that God Himself and the apostles took.

expand to see more

The Anabaptist-Quaker prohibition of all oath-taking misreads the Lord Jesus's words in the Sermon on the Mount. Swear not at all (Matthew 5:34) is understood by the Reformed-confessional tradition (and the broader majority-Christian tradition) to forbid the casual, profane, evasive, and false oath-taking of the Pharisaic practice. The Pharisees had developed an elaborate system of swearing by heaven, earth, Jerusalem, the temple, the gold of the temple, one's own head, etc., creating gradations of binding-ness that permitted evasion (an oath by one thing was binding, an oath by another was not). Christ cuts through this entirely: the Christian's word should be so reliable that his plain yes and no require no reinforcing oath (Matthew 5:37). But this does not forbid the solemn lawful oath taken in truth before God in appropriate settings. God Himself swears by His own name (Hebrews 6:13-17); the LORD commands His people to swear by His name (Deuteronomy 6:13); Paul takes oaths (Romans 1:9; 2 Corinthians 1:23; Galatians 1:20). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive Reformed-confessional doctrine (Westminster XXII): lawful oaths and vows in appropriate settings (courts of law, ordination, marriage, covenant-membership, civil office) are legitimate and sometimes required; the Christian's ordinary speech is plain truth requiring no oath; the casual, profane, and evasive oath-taking that Christ forbade is rejected.

Hebrew Roots

Westminster XXII; God swears by His name (Hebrews 6:13-17); Deuteronomy 6:13; Christ forbids casual/profane/evasive oaths (Matthew 5:34-37), not the solemn lawful oath.
